32_marg1501: All wisdom, etc. Jerome says that he found the book of Jesus the son of Sirach among the Hebrews, entitled not Ecclesiasticus, as among the Latins, but Parables; and with it were joined Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs, so that it matched Solomon not only in the number of books but in the kind of their matter. But the book of Wisdom he did not find among them; rather it smacks of Greek eloquence, and some affirm that it is Philo’s. Ecclesiasticus, like Ecclesiastes, is most useful to the Church; the name means one who gathers or collects, as the other means a preacher. But Ecclesiastes is referred to Christ, Ecclesiasticus to any preacher, who for the excellence of his virtues is called Panaretos, that is, capable of all the virtues. Its clearness and its Latinity are so great that it is its own commentary.
32_marg1502: All wisdom, etc. Rabanus. He begins from the eternal wisdom of God, which is Christ, who is always with the Father before the ages, according to that: “In the beginning was the Word: and the Word was with God,” etc.

Of the other it is written: “The fear of the Lord is holy, enduring for ever and ever.” For each one fears lest he lose good things and the presence of God, which he desires to enjoy for ever; of which it is said: The fear of the Lord shall delight the heart. 32_marg1849: The frankincense: frankincense, as they say, is a tree in Arabia like the laurel in bark and leaf, giving off a juice like the almond’s, which is gathered twice a year, namely in autumn and spring. For the autumn gathering it is prepared by cutting the bark in the heat of summer; a fat foam leaps out which thickens and hardens; where the nature of the place requires, a palm mat catches it, and what has clung to the tree is scraped off with iron. So it looks full of bark; the purest is the white frankincense. The second vintage is prepared in winter by cutting the bark; this comes out red and is not to be compared with the first. That of a young tree is whiter, but that of an old one more fragrant; what has hung from it in a round drop is called male. The frankincense-bearing region is called Sarma, inaccessible on every side, with rocks on the road and shoals of the sea on the right. Sarma means ‘mystery’. The trees grow of their own accord, and they signify those who work of their own will, not from the compulsion of the law. When the trees are cut a tear flows, because the pierced hearts of the humble send forth pure prayer to God.

32_marg1851: Balm: the balsam tree used to grow only in Judaea, within twenty acres; but after the Romans took possession of Judaea it was spread over wide hills. In stock it is like the vine; in leaves like rue, but whiter and always remaining. The tree’s wood is called balsam-wood (xylobalsamum), its fruit or seed carpobalsamum, its juice opobalsamum, because when the bark is struck with iron bonds a drop of excellent fragrance distils through the hollows; for a hollow in Greek is called opē. Its drop is adulterated by mixing it with cyprus oil or honey. But it is proved to be without honey if it curdles with milk; without oil if, dropped into water or mixed with it, it is easily dissolved, and if woollen garments soiled with it are not stained. The adulterated kind does not curdle like milk, floats on water like oil, and stains a woollen garment. Pure balm cannot be held in the hand under a burning sun. Balsam trees are tended like vineyards and held up with props; for they are more like the vine than the myrtle, marked by lasting foliage, standing two cubits high. The seed has the taste of wine and a reddish colour. The branch, thicker than the myrtle’s, sweats balm at a fixed time of the year. Farmers are accustomed to cut it with sharp stones or knives of bone, for the touch of iron is harmful. Through the cuts flows a juice of excellent fragrance, and the tears, dripping beautifully, are gathered little by little with wool into horns. The chief favour is owed to the tear, the second to the seed, the third to the bark, the least to the wood. Christ too, humble in the flesh but full of grace and power, was wounded for our iniquities and poured out for us the sacraments of life and salvation. Whence: “and my odour is as the purest balm.”

32_marg1965: Like to him that catcheth: it signifies that the deceitful dreams of the demons often mock men and draw them into errors unless they are cautiously discerned. Whence: “What can be made clean by the unclean? and what truth can come from that which is false?” Hence it is commanded in the law: “you shall not observe dreams” nor divinations. Yet sometimes revelations come through dreams. Whence Gregory: it must be known, moreover, that the images of dreams touch the mind in six ways. For sometimes they arise from fulness of the belly or from emptiness, sometimes from illusion, sometimes from thought and illusion together, sometimes from revelation, sometimes from thought and revelation together. The first two we all know by experience; the rest we find in the Scriptures. For unless dreams came through the illusion of the devil, the wise man would never say: “dreams have deceived many,” etc.; and elsewhere: “You shall not divine nor observe dreams.” Dreams are shown to be very detestable which are joined to auguries. And because dreams come from thought together with illusion, it is written: “Dreams follow many cares.” But through revelation Joseph saw in a dream that he would be set over his brothers; and Joseph is warned to take the child and his mother into Egypt. And because dreams sometimes come from thought and revelation, Daniel, setting out Nabuchodonosor’s vision, began from the root of the thought: “Thou, O king, didst begin to think in thy bed, what should come to pass hereafter,” etc. Dreams, then, are hard to trust, because it does not easily appear from what impulse they come. But the saints discern illusions and revelations by a certain inward taste, so that they know what they receive from the good spirit and what they suffer from illusion.

32_marg1979: Seven times as much: namely, a perfect reward. The number seven is perfect because it shows the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and because it takes in the inner and outer substance of man: the soul in three, the body in four. Whence: “Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with thy whole strength,” etc.; and the body is made of four elements. The renewal of man can also be figured in seven, because he will be incorruptible in body and immortal in soul. By seven too the present life is designated, as the future by eight.
